text: If you only look at the big headline number — “Over 1,000 anti-trans bills introduced this year!” — it sounds like a one-off spike, a bad storm we just have to ride out. But this isn’t the weather. It’s infrastructure. The anti-trans legislative pile-on has been built out, brick by brick, for more than a decade. It didn’t start with Trump 2.0. It didn’t pause under Biden. And it’s not limited to the “obvious” horrors like banning HRT for kids. The project is bigger: make it harder for trans people to exist anywhere — in schools, in public space, in data, in law, in history. That’s what inequality looks like when it’s running at scale: not one big law, but a whole operating system. In 2013, a six-year-old Colorado girl named Coy Mathis won a landmark ruling after her school tried to kick her out of the girls’ bathroom. State officials found that denying her access was discrimination under Colorado’s civil-rights law, according to ABC News coverage at the time. The backlash came fast. By 2016, North Carolina passed HB2, the infamous “bathroom bill,” locking public bathrooms to birth certificates and blocking local LGBTQ protections. The same organization’s 2024 research (published in partnership with academic researchers) found that anti-trans laws causally increased suicide attempts among trans and nonbinary youth by up to 72%.
